newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Big names of crime in Paris's La Sante prison.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Big names of crime in Paris's La Sante prison.

text.p: Guerrilla Carlos the Jackal, Nazi collaborator Paul Touvier and Japan's Issey Sagawa, who ate his girlfriend, have something in common -- they all served time in Paris's La Sante prison.
Tracking their footsteps reveals a teeming edifice packed with 1,500 inmates, renowned for its big-name prisoners and some spectacular escapes.

La Sante, used for prisoners awaiting trial, is one of France's biggest jails. Some of its cells have been virtually untouched since it was built in 1867 though its VIP wing and isolation sections boast a fresh coat of pastel pink, cream and green paint.
Its cells play host to a wide range of political beliefs -- anarchists, communists, royalists, Nazi collaborators, resistance fighters and Algerian nationalists.

"From this point on you are officially in custody," said deputy-governor Andre Varignan reassuringly after passing through the two main gates leading off La Sante (Health) Street, some way south of the Latin Quarter.
A short flight of steps leads up to the airy and quiet medical wing, where VIPs -- prison officials know them as "the specials" -- are lodged in private cells below a glass roof.

Loik Le Floch-Prigent, ex-chairman of SNCF railways, Jacques Crozemarie, former head of the cancer research association, and other fallen luminaries share the floor with inmates undergoing medical treatment.
SPECIAL HANDLING FOR VIPS
The green pastel doors open into the VIP cells, whose 10 square metres (110 sq ft) are barely big enough to contain a bed, metal chair, table, lavatory and sink.
Prison officials are less than overjoyed by the news coverage this section has generated, especially since a wave of corruption probes rocked political and business establishments.

"The media always talks about this section, but we don't give it overriding importance. It's not on the basis of people like Le Floch-Prigent that we decide how the prison should be run," said La Sante governor Yves Tigoulet.

"We manage these people a bit differently because they are not used to meeting offenders every day, so they are a bit fragile psychologically. Some inmates could be tempted to swindle them. They can be a bit naive," he said.

Two floors down, a low ceiling makes for an oppressive atmosphere in the isolation and disciplinary section where Carlos, seized by the secret services two years ago, is housed alongside Corsican guerrillas, rapists and hunger strikers.
Anytime the likes of Carlos are escorted to the showers or to the exercise yard, floors have to be cleared and extra guards mobilised to prevent any contact with other inmates.
"You don't move Carlos the way you shift a petty thief who stole a hen from a farm," Tigoulet said.
It was from a prison courtyard that Nadine Vaujour, flying a helicopter, snatched her bank robber husband Michel a decade ago.

In 1978, France's "public enemy number one" Jacques Mesrine and an acolyte used a gun and tear-gas to flee to freedom. And two years ago, a rapist sawed through the bars of his cell window and let himself down to the ground with a rope.
Away from the high-security section, "ordinary" prisoners sleep up to four in a cell in areas which have changed little since La Sante was built.

The cells are crowded and the walls virtually covered by clothes, bags and other odds-and-ends hanging from hooks. Several cell doors are open and prisoners lounge about or lie on their bunk-beds, smoking and chatting.

In the dank-smelling Bloc D, three floors of catwalks and cells give out on a shaft closed off by a dirty glass roof, steel bars and mesh wiring. The sound of drills echoes down the corridors as volunteers do repair work.
USER-FRIENDLY PRISON

"We often leave gates open, there is more human contact here," said a guard who would not be named. "La Sante is different because this place is user-friendly -- although perhaps that's not the right word for a prison," he added.
But he complained that sometimes there was only one guard for every 100 inmates, against one for 40 in most other jails.

Most prisoners at La Sante, where some 60 percent are foreigners, are allowed to walk alone to an appointment with their lawyer or with the jail dentist. They show a permit at each gate and guards wave them through.
But not all are convinced of the prison's "user-friendliness".
"I'd say that guards who behave very properly towards us are a minority," said one inmate who had served two years of a 10-year sentence for drugs charges.

"When there starts to be tension in the jail, if people mobilise on a grievance, very quickly the guards get edgy and things get even more tense," said the prisoner, who could not be named under prison regulations.
Poet Guillaume Apollinaire, held for a week at La Sante in September, 1911, on suspicion of helping an art robber, penned a few lines on his ordeal.
"I listen to the sounds of the city
And, prisoner without a horizon,
I see nothing but a hostile sky
And the naked walls of my prison."
